text: Welcome back. This is the last history day before we open the novel. Today’s reading tells about October 1943, when the Nazis planned to arrest all the Jewish people in Denmark, and what ordinary Danes did about it. It’s a story about fear, and about courage. When you finish today, you’ll be ready for the book.

Today’s reading move is putting things side by side. You’ve read four short passages this week, and each one explains a little of the next. As you read today, look back at the other three. Ask how the occupation, the star law, and the king help explain what happened in October 1943.

Choose your sentence. Both are run together, with capitals missing. Today the model is about fishermen and the sea. Look at which words in it are names of peoples and countries. Then make your sentence into two clean sentences, each with a capital at the front and an end mark at the back.

Today’s word work is review, with a twist. Some of what you see is already correct, and some isn’t. Your job is to tap only the mistakes. That means reading every item carefully, even the ones that look fine at first glance. Careful readers check before they change.

Three spans are finished, and their lamps are lit. Today you lay the last four planks. When the final one is down, the bridge reaches the far shore, the shore of our new book. Read each meaning, choose the part that fits, and watch the bridge reach across.

Today’s words come from the story of the rescue. Each one names a part of what happened: a warning, a plan, a secret journey. Read the sentence above each word, and picture the moment it describes. Then guess, and flip to check. You’ll meet ideas like these again in the novel.

This is a draft with a few mistakes in it. Some sentences use the wrong form of a stand-in word, and some are already right. Read each one out loud. When something sounds off, try swapping in he, or him, to check. Tap only the sentences that need fixing.

These words come from a draft, and some are misspelled. The mistakes are mostly in the middle of the word, where the vowels go soft and quiet. Say each word slowly, then picture how it really looks. Tap only the ones that are wrong, and leave the correct ones alone.

Today’s Courage Watch is about remembering. Almost everyone in Denmark’s rescue story is gone now: the fishermen, the families, the king. One kind of courage is choosing not to forget them, and not to forget the people who were hurt. The author of our new book wrote it so that we would remember. Reading it is how you join in.

Today’s passage has a warning, a time of hiding, and a journey across the sea. Watch for all the different kinds of people who helped. Not one hero, but many. When you reach the pause questions, think about what each person risked. And watch for the German man who sent the warning.

Time for the week’s last writing. The first two questions are about the rescue itself. The third asks you to look back across all four readings, so think about the whole week, not just today. Then take your last step in this week’s writing project.

The last question asks what made Denmark’s rescue so unusual. To answer it well, you need to compare. Think about what happened to Jewish people in other countries, and then what happened in Denmark. Name a specific fact from each side. A comparison is only as strong as its facts.

Next week, you’ll write claims about Number the Stars. Today you practice choosing. Write a claim on two different topics, then ask which one you could give the most reasons for. The best claim isn’t always the one you feel most strongly about. It’s the one you have the most to say about.
Transaction. A trade, or an exchange, between people.
Prolong. To make something last longer.
Transcript. A written copy of what someone said.
Pronounce. To say a word out loud.
